stem: A client in the continental United States asks when solar ultraviolet (UV) rays tend to be strongest during daylight saving time. Which response by the nurse is correct?

options.D: UV intensity does not vary with time of day

rationale: CDC states that in the continental United States, UV rays tend to be strongest from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. during daylight saving time (9 a.m. to 3 p.m. during standard time). Therefore A is correct. UV exposure also occurs on cloudy and cool days, and intensity varies with time of day.
educational_objective: Teach clients when solar UV exposure tends to be strongest and reinforce that cloud cover does not eliminate UV exposure.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_locator: Practice sun safety: continental U.S. UV rays strongest 10 a.m.-4 p.m. daylight saving time (9 a.m.-3 p.m. standard time); protection is important all year and UV rays can reach people on cloudy and cool days
source_claim_supported: In the continental United States, UV rays tend to be strongest from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. during daylight saving time, and cloudy conditions do not eliminate UV exposure.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

correction_summary: Specified continental U.S. and daylight saving time so the 10 a.m.-4 p.m. interval is not presented as a universal global rule. Added the standard-time nuance to the rationale and replaced absurd seasonal distractors with errors directly contradicted by current CDC guidance.
audit_findings: A exactly matches current CDC guidance under the conditions stated in the stem. B, C, and D contradict CDC guidance. The geographic/timekeeping qualifiers eliminate unsupported universal precision. No second defensible answer, cueing, or unresolved source conflict remains.
